screens.title: What is a Game Loop?
screens.narratorSegment: A game loop is a program structure that repeats without stopping while the game runs. It continuously polls for input, advances game logic, and redraws the screen. This contrasts with typical event-driven apps that wait and remain idle between events. The loop’s purpose is to ensure every element that needs to change — character positions, physics simulations, AI decisions, timers — is updated in a steady rhythm. Consider a simple simulation: if the loop didn’t run continuously, moving objects would freeze until the next input. A good mental model is the game’s heartbeat: each tick processes input, applies rules, and produces a visual snapshot. That snapshot becomes the player’s current view. A common misconception is that rendering must be done only when something changes; while that can be true for some UIs, most games redraw each frame because small, continuous changes like smooth movement and animation must be shown immediately. Understanding this definition helps you place logic correctly and prevents timing bugs later on. How would a paused loop change your game’s behavior? Reflect on that to see why the loop must run reliably.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What is a Game Loop?
Core Concept

What is a Game Loop?

A repeating runtime cycle that drives all time-dependent behavior in a game.

Analogy
Think of the loop as a heartbeat: each tick keeps the world alive and synchronized.
Common misconception
Believing rendering only on change is enough. Games usually redraw every frame for smooth animation and predictable timing.
Why it matters
Continuous updates ensure animations, physics, and timers progress consistently over time.
Concrete Example
A character with a velocity needs the loop to update its position every tick. Without the loop, position would never change unless triggered by input events.
Key Takeaway

The loop is the game’s heartbeat: steady updates produce smooth, predictable gameplay.

screens.title: Loop Phases: Input, Update, Render
screens.narratorSegment: The game loop is often organized into three phases that repeat each frame: Input Processing, Game State Update, and Rendering. Input Processing reads device states — which keys are pressed, the mouse position, or controller buttons — and translates those into actions or commands. This must happen first so the frame’s update reflects the latest player intent rather than a frame late. Game State Update then runs game logic: move characters, run AI decisions, apply physics, detect collisions, update timers and scores. This is where delta time is applied so that motion and timers scale with real time. Finally, Rendering draws the current, updated state to the screen so the player sees the results immediately. If rendering came before updating, the player would see the previous frame’s state, introducing a one-frame delay. A common beginner mistake is mixing input handling inside rendering code or updating visuals before logic; keep responsibilities separated. This clear order simplifies reasoning about when to apply forces, when to read input, and when to produce the final frame. Think about the visible result: the player’s inputs should affect what they see in the same frame.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Loop Phases
Process Flow

Input → Update → Render

This order ensures player actions apply to the same frame’s update and rendering.

Input Processing
Query devices and queue actions. Capture all inputs that occurred since the last frame.
Game State Update
Advance physics, AI, timers, and collisions using delta time for consistency.
Rendering
Draw the updated state as the final snapshot the player sees this frame.
Scenario
If a jump button is pressed this frame, Input records it, Update applies vertical velocity, and Render shows the character moving. If input were processed after update, the jump would be delayed by one frame.
Common mistake
Mixing rendering with input reading can introduce subtle bugs. Keep responsibilities separated to avoid frame-dependent errors.
Key Takeaway

Process input first, update logic second with delta time, and render last for a responsive frame.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Minimal C++ Loop
Code Walkthrough

Minimal C++ Loop

This example shows the pattern without external libraries so the timing logic is clear.

#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>
#include <thread>

void ProcessInput() { /* read devices */ }
void Update(double deltaTime) { /* apply movement, physics */ }
void Render() { /* draw current state */ }

int main() {
  bool running = true;
  auto lastFrameTime = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();

  while (running) {
    auto current = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    std::chrono::duration<double> dt = current - lastFrameTime;
    double deltaTime = dt.count();
    lastFrameTime = current;

    ProcessInput();
    Update(deltaTime);
    Render();

    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(10));
  }
  return 0;
}
Explanation
  • Time is measured each frame so deltaTime reflects real seconds between frames.
  • Update receives deltaTime so movement and timers scale with elapsed time.
  • The sleep call is optional and only helps prevent busy-waiting in simple examples.
Pro tip
Initialize lastFrameTime before the loop to avoid a large delta at startup. Update it at each loop end.
Key Takeaway

Measure time each frame and pass delta time into update to keep logic consistent.

screens.title: Delta Time Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Delta time is simply the real elapsed time between the current frame and the previous one, usually measured in seconds. Its practical role is to scale time-dependent calculations so they reflect actual time rather than frame count. For example, a character that moves at 100 units per second should move 100 times deltaTime units each frame. If the frame rate halves, deltaTime doubles and the per-frame movement increases proportionally, keeping real-world motion unchanged. Without delta time, movement tied to frames will run faster on high-FPS machines and slower on low-FPS machines. A common mistake is to forget to multiply speeds by deltaTime or to use integer types that truncate fractional seconds, which leads to jerky or incorrect movement. Another pitfall is trusting a constant frame duration; that assumption fails under changing C P U/G P U load. Delta time makes logic resilient: scores, animations, timers, and physics depend on elapsed time, not the number of frames. When you test your loop, deliberately change the loop timing or add sleeps to watch how deltaTime preserves consistent behavior. Delta Time Explained means delta time is elapsed seconds between frames and is multiplied into movement and timer calculations to ensure frame-rate independent behavior.. In practical terms, what delta time is and why it prevents speed variance across frame rates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Delta Time Explained
Definition

What is delta time?

The elapsed time in seconds between two consecutive frames, used to scale all time-dependent updates.

Formula
movementThisFrame = speedInUnitsPerSecond * deltaTime
Common pitfall
Forgetting to multiply by delta time makes behavior dependent on frame count, not real time.
Concrete Example
If speed is 100 units/second and deltaTime is 0.016 seconds, movement is 1.6 units this frame. If deltaTime becomes 0.033 seconds at lower FPS, movement becomes 3.3 units this frame. Over one real second both sum to ~100 units.
Pro tip
Use double precision when accumulating elapsed time to avoid precision loss over long runs.
Key Takeaway

Multiply durations by delta time for frame-rate independent motion and timers.

screens.title: Applying Delta Time to Movement
screens.narratorSegment: Here is a small snippet that shows the core idea of applying delta time to movement. The important parts are: a speed expressed in units per second, an accumulator for position, and updating position by speed multiplied by deltaTime. This ensures the object moves the same real-world distance per second regardless of frame timing. When reviewing the code, notice the units are seconds for delta time and units per second for speed. Avoid using frame-count-based increments such as adding a fixed number each frame. Also consider using a separate accumulator for sub-second timers to trigger events after a set real duration. Beginners sometimes mistakenly clamp delta time or assume it is constant; instead, code defensively to handle occasional spikes but prefer smoothing only when necessary. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Applying Delta Time
Code Example
// Speed in units per second
double speed = 100.0; 
double position = 0.0;

// each frame
void Update(double deltaTime) {
  position += speed * deltaTime; // movement scaled by elapsed time
}
Why this works
  • Speed is per-second, so multiplying by seconds yields per-frame distance.
  • Summing per-frame distances over one real second equals speed * 1s.
  • Avoid hard-coded per-frame deltas like adding a fixed integer each frame.
Key Takeaway

Use speed in units per second and multiply by delta time for correct movement across frame rates.

screens.title: With and Without Delta Time
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing behavior with and without delta time clarifies its importance. Without delta time, many beginners update positions by adding a constant per frame. That ties simulation speed directly to frame count: twice the frames, twice the speed. With delta time, movement and timers are scaled by elapsed seconds, so the same real-world time produces the same outcome regardless of FPS. For a concrete example, imagine a character speed of 100 units per second. At 60 FPS, deltaTime is about 0.0167, so each frame moves about 1.67 units; at 30 FPS, deltaTime is about 0.0333 so each frame moves about 3.33 units; total per second remains about 100 units. A typical debugging exercise is to artificially sleep inside the loop and observe that the with-delta implementation preserves pacing while the without-delta implementation slows or speeds up erratically. Remember that delta time must be used consistently across movement, timers, and animation time advancement. This comparison is a practical test you can run in the console starter project to see the difference first-hand. Without Delta Time
Position incremented by a fixed amount each frame. Result: speed varies with FPS.
Problem
High-FPS systems run logic faster; low-FPS systems run slower, causing inconsistent gameplay.
With Delta Time
Position incremented by speed * deltaTime each frame. Result: consistent real-time behavior.
Benefit
Movement and timers remain predictable and independent of frame rate.
Check your understanding

Try adding sleep delays and watch which implementation preserves speed.

screens.title: Time Management and Frame Rate Limiting
screens.narratorSegment: In simple console or prototype loops you may add a short sleep to avoid wasting C P U cycles. The example uses a small sleep to prevent 100 percent C P U usage when there is no real rendering work. In production engines, more sophisticated systems such as vertical sync, adaptive waiting strategies, or the rendering A P I's present call handle pacing. The important teaching point here is that timing decisions are orthogonal to correctness: whether you sleep or not, delta time must still be computed and used. Sleep introduces larger delta times when the loop resumes, so your code should tolerate occasional spikes and not assume a constant delta. Beginners often confuse frame limiting with making logic frame-rate dependent; keep the separation clear: frame limiting controls how often frames are produced, while delta time normalizes logic to real time. If you want smooth physics, consider smaller maximum delta clamps to guard against very large time steps, but avoid silently dropping significant time without handling the consequences. In short, use sleep or engine pacing to manage resources, but always drive game logic from accurate elapsed time measurements.

Architecture

Frame Rate Limiting

Use simple sleeps in prototypes. In engines, present calls or VSync handle pacing. Regardless, compute delta each frame.

Resource note

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Game Time Counter
Starter Code
#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>
#include <thread>

float gameTime = 0.0f;

void ProcessInput() { }
void Update(double deltaTime) {
  gameTime += (float)deltaTime; // add elapsed seconds
  static float printTimer = 0.0f;
  printTimer += (float)deltaTime;
  if (printTimer >= 1.0f) {
    std::cout << "Current Game Time: " << gameTime << " seconds
";
    printTimer -= 1.0f;
  }
}
void Render() { }

int main() { /* time loop as before */ }
Implementation Notes
  • Use floating point types for time accumulators to keep fractional seconds.
  • Print periodically using an internal timer rather than every frame to reduce console noise.
  • Verify that gameTime increases steadily when you add artificial delays.
Key Takeaway

Accumulate delta time into a gameTime variable to produce a stable, real-time clock for the game.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Debugging Tips
screens.narratorSegment: Timing bugs are common when first building game loops. One frequent error is forgetting to initialize last frame time before entering the loop, which can cause a large initial delta and a big jump in the first update. Another is using integer types for time accumulators, which lose fractional seconds and produce coarse updates. Omitting delta time entirely leads to performance-dependent behavior. Mixing input reads inside rendering can cause missed inputs or race conditions. To debug, add console prints for delta time and gameTime to observe whether values are steady or spiking. If you see irregular spikes, check for blocking calls or long sleeps. Use smaller sleep durations or engine-provided timing where appropriate. When physics appears unstable under variable delta times, consider fixed-step sub-updates inside the update phase: accumulate elapsed time and run several fixed-size steps to maintain stable simulation while still tracking total elapsed time. These strategies come from the same source material and will help you find and fix timing-related issues quickly as you explore loop implementations. fullNarratorScript:
Every interactive game runs on a repeating cycle that keeps the world alive. In this lesson you will learn what that cycle is, why it must run continuously, and how three simple phases — input, update, and render — coordinate to create responsive, predictable gameplay. We’ll also cover delta time, the small but critical value that makes movement and timers consistent across different machines. You will see a minimal C++ example that captures the pattern, and a short activity that demonstrates how to keep game time advancing steadily no matter how fast frames are produced. Understanding the loop helps you reason about where to read player controls, where to apply physics or AI, and where to draw the updated scene. As you follow the examples, notice the difference between event-driven programs that wait for input and games that never pause. By the end of this chapter you will be able to sketch a basic loop, implement it in a console program, and explain why delta time must be applied to any time-dependent calculation. Consider how this heartbeat keeps animation smooth and gameplay fair across systems.

These objectives map to concrete skills you’ll practice. First, you will explain the purpose and structure of a game loop so you can reason about where and why continuous updates are needed. Second, you will identify the loop’s three core phases — input, update, render — and describe what each phase must do each frame, which lets you place logic where it belongs. Third, you will implement a basic C++ game loop structure using time measurement and a repeating while loop so you can prototype interactive behavior even in a console program. Finally, you will understand delta time and apply it to movement or timers to make game logic frame-rate independent. Each objective pairs conceptual understanding with a hands-on example. For example, implementing the starter console loop helps you see how delta time keeps a counter progressing at the same real-world speed no matter the frame rate. These skills form the foundation for building predictable game behavior and debugging timing issues later in engine work.

We’ll connect the learning goals to Bloom’s taxonomy so you can track progress. First level: Learn — you will recall the loop’s three phases and the role of delta time. Second: Understand — you will explain why continuous updates are necessary and why input must be processed before state updates. Third: Apply — you will implement a simple C++ loop that measures elapsed time and uses it to update a counter or a moving object. Fourth: Master — you will reason about when to add frame limiting or when to use engine timing systems in larger projects. Each objective includes a practical check: run the starter console program, observe the printed game time, and vary system load to ensure the counter advances consistently. Framing tasks this way keeps you focused on both conceptual understanding and reproducible coding practice. When you complete the hands-on activity, you should be able to explain failure modes you observe if delta time is omitted.

A game loop is a program structure that repeats without stopping while the game runs. It continuously polls for input, advances game logic, and redraws the screen. This contrasts with typical event-driven apps that wait and remain idle between events. The loop’s purpose is to ensure every element that needs to change — character positions, physics simulations, AI decisions, timers — is updated in a steady rhythm. Consider a simple simulation: if the loop didn’t run continuously, moving objects would freeze until the next input. A good mental model is the game’s heartbeat: each tick processes input, applies rules, and produces a visual snapshot. That snapshot becomes the player’s current view. A common misconception is that rendering must be done only when something changes; while that can be true for some UIs, most games redraw each frame because small, continuous changes like smooth movement and animation must be shown immediately. Understanding this definition helps you place logic correctly and prevents timing bugs later on. How would a paused loop change your game’s behavior? Reflect on that to see why the loop must run reliably.

The game loop is often organized into three phases that repeat each frame: Input Processing, Game State Update, and Rendering. Input Processing reads device states — which keys are pressed, the mouse position, or controller buttons — and translates those into actions or commands. This must happen first so the frame’s update reflects the latest player intent rather than a frame late. Game State Update then runs game logic: move characters, run AI decisions, apply physics, detect collisions, update timers and scores. This is where delta time is applied so that motion and timers scale with real time. Finally, Rendering draws the current, updated state to the screen so the player sees the results immediately. If rendering came before updating, the player would see the previous frame’s state, introducing a one-frame delay. A common beginner mistake is mixing input handling inside rendering code or updating visuals before logic; keep responsibilities separated. This clear order simplifies reasoning about when to apply forces, when to read input, and when to produce the final frame. Think about the visible result: the player’s inputs should affect what they see in the same frame.

Let’s walk through the minimal C++ loop example provided in the chapter. The program declares a running flag to control the main while loop, and uses high-resolution clocks to measure time between frames. Each iteration computes delta time as the elapsed seconds since the previous frame. Then the loop calls three placeholder functions in order: ProcessInput, Update, and Render. In Update we would pass delta time so game logic scales with real time. The code also illustrates an optional sleep to avoid spinning the C P U at 100 percent while the example runs quickly. This minimal structure intentionally avoids windowing or graphics APIs so you can focus on where timing sits. In practice, each placeholder would call into subsystems — input handling queries OS or library events, update runs world simulations, and render hands data to a graphics A P I or engine. A common confusion for beginners is where to put time initialization: measuring lastFrameTime before entering the loop and updating it at the end of each frame avoids incorrect large deltas at startup. Try reading the code slowly and mapping each comment to the conceptual phase to see the pattern clearly.

Delta time is simply the real elapsed time between the current frame and the previous one, usually measured in seconds. Its practical role is to scale time-dependent calculations so they reflect actual time rather than frame count. For example, a character that moves at 100 units per second should move 100 times deltaTime units each frame. If the frame rate halves, deltaTime doubles and the per-frame movement increases proportionally, keeping real-world motion unchanged. Without delta time, movement tied to frames will run faster on high-FPS machines and slower on low-FPS machines. A common mistake is to forget to multiply speeds by deltaTime or to use integer types that truncate fractional seconds, which leads to jerky or incorrect movement. Another pitfall is trusting a constant frame duration; that assumption fails under changing C P U/G P U load. Delta time makes logic resilient: scores, animations, timers, and physics depend on elapsed time, not the number of frames. These compact concepts are the essential takeaways to remember: the game loop is a continuous cycle of Input, Update, and Render that keeps the game world progressing; input must be processed first so player actions affect the same frame’s update; game state updates should be driven by accurate elapsed time measurements; rendering should draw the updated state as the final step; and delta time is the elapsed seconds between frames and must be multiplied into movement and timers to achieve frame-rate independent behavior. Keep these short rules in mind as you code: always compute delta time each frame, pass it into update logic, and avoid tying behavior directly to frame counts.
